title: Research Bite #48: Mathematical Etudes
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Research Bite summarises Colin Foster's paper on mathematical etudes, which borrows its central analogy from music: an etude is a piece that gives a performer extensive practice on one technique while also being aesthetically satisfying to play. Foster's claim is that mathematics tasks can do the same — embedding heavy practice of a well-defined technique inside a richer, investigative problem — which dissolves the standard trade-off teachers feel between drill-based procedural fluency and rich, exploratory mathematics. Students get the extensive practice required for high-stakes assessment and the purposeful context that shows why a technique matters, with fluency encouraged by drawing attention away from procedural minutiae toward a bigger problem. Barton highlights two classroom payoffs (etudes are less tedious to mark and dignify all students with access to higher-order thinking) and one caution: designing a well-constructed etude takes significantly more creative effort than pulling routine exercises from a textbook.
points: Foster's etude analogy dissolves a false binary: procedural-fluency drill and rich investigative mathematics don't have to be separate lessons — a well-designed task embeds extensive technique practice inside an aesthetically satisfying, purposeful problem.

Fluency is encouraged indirectly, by drawing learners' attention away from the minutiae of the procedure and toward a bigger, more interesting problem, which Foster and Barton both note also makes the tasks less tedious to mark.

The approach dignifies all learners with access to higher-order mathematical thinking rather than gating it behind prior procedural mastery — confident students can extend the problem while others focus on the narrower technique.

The tradeoff is real: designing a genuinely well-constructed etude that embeds practice inside a rich context takes significantly more creative effort from the teacher than assigning routine textbook exercises.
quotes: Mathematical études," authored by Colin Foster, proposes an innovative approach to mathematics education by embedding opportunities for procedural fluency practice within richer, investigative contexts, drawing an analogy from musical études to harmonise traditional drill-and-practice with progressive, exploratory learning.

Études help teachers harmonise the apparently conflicting requirements of teaching. They combine the development of procedural fluency (necessary for high-stakes assessment) with offering richer, investigative mathematical experiences.

They facilitate task design that embeds extensive practice of a specific, well-defined mathematical technique within a richer, aesthetically pleasing mathematical context. The tasks become more purposeful and authentically mathematical for learners, illustrating why a technique is useful and important.

Fluency may be encouraged by deliberately drawing the learners' attention away from the "minutiae of the procedure" and focusing instead on a bigger, more interesting problem. Études are often less tedious for the teacher to mark and more interesting for both the teacher and the learners.

The approach dignifies all learners with opportunities to think mathematically, avoiding the practice of keeping them away from rich higher-level-thinking tasks until they have mastered prior procedures. For confident learners, there is scope to extend the problem, making the étude mathematically quite open.

Caution is needed because designing a well-constructed mathematical étude that successfully embeds extensive practice within an aesthetically satisfying and rich context requires significant creative effort by the teacher, unlike using standard routine exercises.
